Import.description: Imports other configuration files, as Spring's spring.config.import does. An imported file overrides the one importing it; a relative path resolves against the directory of the file importing it; an optional: prefix skips a file that does not exist

Name.description: is the application name, preferably globally unique, such as team.system.app.

Profiles.description: Which profiles are active, as Spring's spring.profiles.active is: one name, a comma-separated string, or a list, where a later one overrides an earlier one. It ranks below --profile and XONE_PROFILE, and may be written in the main configuration file only

Version.description: is the application version, such as v1.2.0.

BeegoLogs.description: routes beego's own logs package into slog. On by default. Beego's logs writes plain text to the console: a service whose logs are collected as JSON has those lines fall out of every field-based query, and an application using beego's logs as its own logger has all of its logging fall out. With this on, every line beego writes becomes one slog record (the message under message, beego's eight levels folded onto slog's four), so XLog governs the format and the level for the whole process. It replaces whatever the application configured on beego's logger, so turn it off to keep a setup of your own -- a file adapter with rotation, say. beego's logger is process-wide, as its router is, and the first assembly settles this for the process; an instance assembling later with a different value is told that value was ignored. These lines carry no trace_id: beego's logs API has no ctx to take one from. A handler that wants one writes through slog with the request's ctx (c.Ctx.Request.Context()).

Host.description: is the listen address. Defaults to 0.0.0.0.

IdleTimeout.description: bounds how long a keep-alive connection may sit idle. Defaults to 60s, must be > 0. Same reasoning as ReadHeaderTimeout: 0 falls back to ReadTimeout (itself 0 by default), which means idle connections are never reclaimed. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

Log.description: enables the access log middleware. On by default. It replaces whatever access logging the application had of its own (a filter pair at BeforeRouter / AfterExec is the usual shape). Leaving both in place writes every request twice, with two different sets of field names; remove the application's.

LogQuery.description: records the query string in the access log, as the query field. Off by default. Query strings often carry credentials: GET /login?token=..., signed links, an OAuth callback's code. With it on, fields are masked by the same rules as a form body; a name missing from the word list (code, for instance) still goes through in the clear, so add it with middleware.AddSensitiveFields.

LogRequestBody.description: records the request body in the access log. Off by default. Recording a body means buffering its first 256KB and masking every field, which costs enough and risks enough to be a decision. Before turning it on, make sure the sensitive words are complete (middleware.AddSensitiveFields; the rules are under "Access log" in xbeego/README.md).

LogRequestHeaders.description: records the request headers in the access log, as the request_headers field. Off by default. With it on, credential-bearing values are masked: the listed ones such as Authorization, Cookie and X-Api-Key, plus any name containing a sensitive word; values that are URLs (Referer) lose their query string. Add business headers outside the list with middleware.AddSensitiveHeaders.

LogResponseBody.description: records the response body in the access log. Off by default.

LogResponseHeaders.description: records the response headers in the access log, as the response_headers field. Off by default. Masking works as it does for request headers: the listed ones such as Set-Cookie, plus any name containing a sensitive word, have their values masked.

LogSkipPaths.description: lists paths that are not access-logged. Empty by default. A path ending in / matches by prefix, anything else matches exactly. With Metric on, MetricPath is added automatically and needs no entry.

Metric.description: enables the metrics middleware. On by default. When on, MetricPath (/metrics by default) is served by the framework and needs no route of your own. It is answered before the request reaches beego, so beego's router never sees it: an application that registers a route on that path has to drop it or move this one, and until it does, startup fails with an error naming MetricPath rather than the route being shadowed without a word.

MetricPath.description: is the path of the metrics endpoint. Defaults to /metrics, and must start with / while Metric is on. It is matched on URL.Path exactly, as the access log's SkipPaths does, so a spelling without the leading / would match nothing and leave the endpoint unreachable without a word. That is why it is rejected at startup instead. The framework answers this path in front of beego's router, so a beego route registered on exactly this template fails startup with an error naming this field rather than never being reached, see Metric. A pattern that merely happens to match it (/:page) is left alone: it was never meant to be this endpoint.

Port.description: is the listen port. Defaults to 8080. This is the only listen setting that counts: web.Run is not called, so beego's own httpaddr and httpport in conf/app.conf are read by beego and used by nobody.

ReadHeaderTimeout.description: bounds reading the request headers. Defaults to 10s, must be > 0. This is the main defense against slow-connection attacks: without a limit, a slow client holds a connection indefinitely, and once the connection count is exhausted the whole service is unavailable. Beego sets ReadTimeout and WriteTimeout from a single ServerTimeOut in conf/app.conf (0 by default, that is, no limit at all) and has no setting for the other two; this module does not use beego's server and builds an http.Server from these fields instead. 0 does not mean "use some default": net/http falls back to ReadTimeout, whose default is also 0, so there is no limit at all. Both 0 and negative values are therefore rejected. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

ReadTimeout.description: bounds reading the whole request, body included. Unlimited by default. Unlimited by default because a limit cuts off large uploads. A value matching the business ceiling is better, but only the business knows that value. 0 means unlimited; a negative value fails startup. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

RecoverPanic.description: takes beego's panic recovery over (web.BConfig.RecoverFunc). On by default. Beego recovers panics inside its own router and writes them with its logs package: plain text on stderr, no trace_id, no masking, and the whole thing invisible to the access log and the metrics, which see a 500 with no reason attached. With this on, the framework's own recovery is installed in its place (web.BConfig.RecoverFunc): one ERROR line through slog carrying trace_id, the panic value masked by the same rules as the access log's, and a stack. The response is a bare 500 unless WithRecoverFunc says otherwise. Turning it off leaves beego's recovery as it is. The framework then still catches whatever escapes beego (a panic in middleware mounted with WithMiddleware, for one), since a panic reaching net/http kills the connection with no log at all. What is replaced is the slot beego calls (web.BConfig.RecoverFunc), not its switch. A panic is caught either way: with this off, what beego's recovery lets through is still caught outside beego. beego's own web.BConfig.RecoverPanic -- recoverpanic in conf/app.conf -- decides one thing while this is on. An abort onto a registered error handler (c.Abort("404")) is handed back to the recovery that stood in the slot before, which is the only code that can render a handler registered under a name rather than a status code; with recoverpanic off that recovery declines, and such a response then carries no body. A numeric code is unaffected, being rendered through web.Exception in that case. This is a process-wide setting of beego's, not a per-instance one: two XBeego instances in one process share it, as they share the router, and the first assembly settles it for the process. An instance assembling later with a different value is told that value was ignored.

TLS.description: holds the server certificate and mutual authentication. Off by default: setting both CertFile and KeyFile makes it https.

CertFile.description: is the path to the TLS certificate. It and KeyFile must both be set or both be empty.

ClientCAFile.description: is the CA used to verify client certificates (PEM, several are allowed). Empty by default, meaning no client certificate is requested. Setting it turns on mutual authentication (tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert): the client must present a certificate signed by this CA, and without one -- or with one signed by someone else -- the handshake fails and the request reaches no handler, including framework routes such as /metrics. It can only be set together with CertFile and KeyFile.

KeyFile.description: is the path to the TLS private key.

MinVersion.description: is the lowest TLS version accepted: "1.2" or "1.3", and empty means "1.2". Defaults to "1.2". It applies, and is validated, only when a certificate is configured. Lower versions are not accepted: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 have long been deprecated (RFC 8996).

Trace.description: opens a server span for inbound requests. On by default. It governs the span only. With it off, an incoming traceparent, baggage and forwarded headers are still accepted (under the same trust rules as TrustedProxies), trace_id in the log is the upstream one, and requests sent through xhttp still carry it downstream; the response no longer carries X-Trace-Id back.

TrustedProxies.description: lists which directly connected peers are trusted: only their X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP is used to compute client_ip, and only their forwarded headers (XTrace.ForwardHeaders / ForwardHeaderRules) and baggage are accepted and passed downstream. "Who counts as one of us" is stated here and nowhere else. The default is [private]: loopback, the private ranges, 100.64.0.0/10, and IPv6 ::1 and fc00::/7. Load balancers, Kubernetes ingresses and pods, and sidecars all fall inside those ranges, so however random pod IPs are, they need no listing. For a service exposed directly to the internet the peer is a public address, none of which is trusted, so X-Forwarded-For still cannot forge client_ip. Beego's own ctx.Input.IP() is not used and is not governed by this: it walks X-Forwarded-For from the left and believes whoever sent it (Proxy / IP in server/web/context/input.go). The client_ip in the access log, in the metrics and on the span is computed here instead, by the same algorithm xgin and xecho use, so moving a service between frameworks does not change it. Business code reading ctx.Input.IP() keeps beego's answer; to get the framework's, read the client_ip field of the access log or call xbeego.ClientIP(r). To add ranges on top of the default, write private alongside them (the list replaces the default wholesale); to trust nobody, write []: When the internal network also holds untrusted clients (an office network or VPN users can reach the service directly), do not use private: list the exact ranges. Write IPv4 as 10.0.0.1 or 10.0.0.0/8; an IPv4-mapped IPv6 form such as ::ffff:10.0.0.1 fails startup.

UseH2C.description: enables HTTP/2 without TLS. Off by default. Under TLS, HTTP/2 is automatic and this option is not needed. Prior knowledge only: the client opens with the HTTP/2 preface (gRPC and curl --http2-prior-knowledge both do). The HTTP/1.1 Upgrade: h2c handshake is not supported, and a client sending it gets an ordinary HTTP/1.1 response.

WriteTimeout.description: bounds writing the response. Unlimited by default. Unlimited by default because a limit cuts off SSE, long polling and large downloads. 0 means unlimited; a negative value fails startup. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

XCache.description: is this module's configuration. There are two forms

BufferItems.description: is the size of the internal buffer for Get. It defaults to 64, the value upstream recommends.

DefaultTTL.description: is the expiry used by the package-level Set. It defaults to 5m. 0 means it never expires; a negative value fails startup -- ristretto drops a write with ttl<0 outright. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

MaxCost.description: is the upper bound on the cache's total cost. It defaults to 100000. This package always writes with cost 1, so it is equivalent to "how many entries at most". It is a real cost bound only when C().Set is called directly with a different cost. What is counted here is the cost the caller gives, without ristretto's 56 bytes of internal overhead per entry. When recording cost in bytes, include that in the budget.

Metric.description: says whether to export the hit rate and the other metrics. It defaults to on, as in XGorm / XRedis. It applies per instance: an instance configured with Metric: false does not appear in /metrics and ristretto does not count for it either. The counting is ristretto's own: its Metrics is off by default, and nothing is visible until it is turned on. The cost of turning it on, measured (ristretto v2.4.2, 4 cores): - Memory: about 84KB more resident per instance; plus a table recording write times (for its lifetime histogram, at most 100 thousand entries), about 8-12MB more after more than 100 thousand distinct keys have been written. - CPU: no significant difference in this package's Get / Set benchmarks (p>0.2); ristretto's own 4-goroutine concurrent Get costs about 20ns more per call (110ns -> 131ns, noise +-12%). Turn it off per instance when there are many instances, many entries, and memory matters.

NumCounters.description: is the number of counters used to track access frequency. It defaults to 1000000. Ten times the expected number of entries is a good value: ristretto uses it to decide which keys are worth keeping, and too few makes the admission decision inaccurate and holds the hit rate down.

Debug.description: turns on echo's debug switch (e.Debug). Off by default, same as echo.New(). Keep it off in production. This is not XGin.Mode: gin's Mode is process-wide (gin.SetMode), while this is per instance, so two servers started with WithConfig in one process can differ.

With it off, an incoming traceparent, baggage and forwarded headers are still accepted (under the same trust rules as TrustedProxies), trace_id in the log is the upstream one, and requests sent through xhttp still carry it downstream; the response no longer carries X-Trace-Id back.

TrustedProxies.description: lists which directly connected peers are trusted: only their X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP is used to compute client_ip, and only their forwarded headers (XTrace.ForwardHeaders / ForwardHeaderRules) and baggage are accepted and passed downstream. "Who counts as one of us" is stated here and nowhere else. The default is [private]: loopback, the private ranges, 100.64.0.0/10, and IPv6 ::1 and fc00::/7 (see privateNetworks). Load balancers, Kubernetes ingresses and pods, and sidecars all fall inside those ranges, so however random pod IPs are, they need no listing. For a service exposed directly to the internet the peer is a public address, none of which is trusted, so X-Forwarded-For still cannot forge client_ip. Gin's own default is to trust everyone: anyone sending X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4 decides client_ip. To add ranges on top of the default, write private alongside them (the list replaces the default wholesale); to trust nobody, write []: When the internal network also holds untrusted clients (an office network or VPN users can reach the service directly), do not use private: list the exact ranges. Write IPv4 as 10.0.0.1 or 10.0.0.0/8; an IPv4-mapped IPv6 form such as ::ffff:10.0.0.1 fails startup.

UseH2C.description: enables HTTP/2 without TLS. Off by default. Under TLS, HTTP/2 is automatic and this option is not needed. Prior knowledge only: the client opens with the HTTP/2 preface (gRPC and curl --http2-prior-knowledge both do). The HTTP/1.1 Upgrade: h2c handshake is not supported, and a client sending it gets an ordinary HTTP/1.1 response. The reasoning is under protocols.

WriteTimeout.description: bounds writing the response. Unlimited by default. Unlimited by default because a limit cuts off SSE, long polling and large downloads. 0 means unlimited; a negative value fails startup. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

ZHTranslations.description: translates validator's errors into Chinese. Off by default.

XGinSwagger.description: is the Swagger document metadata. These values live in the configuration rather than in code annotations because they vary by environment: the Host of an integration environment differs from production, while doc annotations are compiled in.

BasePath.description: is the common prefix of every endpoint, such as /api/v1.

Host.description: is the service address shown in the document, such as api.example.com. It defaults to the request's.

Schemes.description: are the supported protocols, such as ["https"]. It defaults to empty: the @schemes from the annotations is kept unless this is set.

Title.description: is the document title. It defaults to XApp.Name.

URLPrefix.description: is the prefix of the Swagger UI mount path, such as /internal. The default mounts at /swagger/*any. It is either empty or starts with / and does not end with /, or startup fails. gin itself is not fussy (measured on v1.12.0: internal and /internal/ are both normalized to /internal/swagger/*any without a panic), but URL() concatenates it as it is, and the resulting internal/swagger/index.html does not match the address it is actually mounted at.

XGorm.description: is this module's configuration. Two forms

CreateBatchSize.description: is how many rows one INSERT carries when Creating a slice. 0 by default: the whole slice in one INSERT. Measured with 10 rows and a setting of 3: both PostgreSQL and MySQL sent 4 INSERTs (3+3+3+1) and all 10 rows were written. Use it for a large slice to stay under the parameter limit of one statement (65535 on PostgreSQL) and the packet size limit (MySQL's max_allowed_packet).

DSN.description: is the connection string. Required. Writing it as "${DB_DSN}" is recommended: credentials do not belong in version control, and a missing one then fails startup. A MySQL DSN that does not write parseTime gets parseTime=true: the driver defaults to false and a DATETIME cannot be scanned into a time.Time (measured with go-sql-driver v1.10.1, one First on a model with CreatedAt reports unsupported Scan). A DSN that writes it wins.

DialTimeout.description: is the connect timeout. Defaults to 500ms. It is injected as timeout for MySQL and as connect_timeout for PostgreSQL (rounded up to whole seconds). At 0 nothing is injected and the driver's own applies (both drivers: no limit). It must not be negative, and neither may any duration below. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

DisableForeignKeyConstraintWhenMigrating.description: keeps AutoMigrate from creating foreign key constraints. false by default, which is GORM's default: foreign keys are created from the associations in the models. It affects migration only, and queries and associations are unchanged: measured with GORM v1.31.2 and PostgreSQL 16 on the two tables of Owner has many Order, the default creates fk_owners_orders and an order with a nonexistent owner_id is rejected; with it on no foreign key is created, that row inserts fine, and Preload("Orders") still finds it. Referential integrity is your code's business from then on. Foreign keys already created are not dropped.

Driver.description: is the driver: mysql / postgres. Defaults to postgres. Other drivers live in modules of their own and register themselves on an anonymous import

IgnoreNotFound.description: decides whether "no record found" is logged as an error. false by default.

Log.description: routes GORM's SQL log into slog. Off by default. When a statement fails, the error field records the server's error code alone (with a separate error_code field) and never its text: measured, MySQL 8.0's 1062 reads Duplicate entry 'a@b.com' for key …, with the parameter value right in it. The error returned to the caller is unchanged.

MaxIdleConns.description: is the maximum number of idle connections. Defaults to 50. 0 means "keep not one idle connection", so every query reconnects, which is usually not what you want. Larger than MaxOpenConns is fine, since database/sql caps it at MaxOpenConns itself.

MaxIdleTime.description: is how long an idle connection may live. Defaults to 5m, and 0 means no limit. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

MaxLifetime.description: is how long a connection may live. Defaults to 5m, and 0 means no limit. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

MaxOpenConns.description: is the maximum number of connections. Defaults to 50.

Metric.description: decides whether the db_pool_* connection pool metrics are exported (connection counts, wait counts, wait durations and so on), labelled with the instance name. On by default. The metrics read sql.DB.Stats() when they are scraped and occupy no goroutine. It applies per instance: an instance with Metric: false does not appear in /metrics.

MySQL.description: applies only when Driver is mysql.

ReadTimeout.description: is the read timeout, the DSN's readTimeout. Defaults to 3s, and 0 injects nothing (so the driver has no limit). (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

WriteTimeout.description: is the write timeout, the DSN's writeTimeout. Defaults to 5s, and 0 injects nothing (so the driver has no limit). (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

Postgres.description: applies only when Driver is postgres.

IdleInTxTimeout.description: disconnects after this long idle inside a transaction. No limit by default. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

LockTimeout.description: is how long to wait for a lock. No limit by default. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

Params.description: holds any other PG runtime parameters, appended to the DSN as they are. pgx's own connection parameters go here too, such as default_query_exec_mode: exec when connecting through PgBouncer's transaction pooling — pgx's default cache_statement uses named prepared statements, and measured against PgBouncer 1.22 in transaction pooling (max_prepared_statements at 0, the default before 1.24), 20 goroutines running 1000 queries produced 701 reports of prepared statement "stmtcache_…" already exists (42P05). The details and the cost of each mode are in xgorm/README.md under "PostgreSQL".

StatementTimeout.description: is how long one statement may run. No limit by default. It is the server's clock and governs how long the server has been executing a statement it received. The PG client side has no read timeout the way MySQL does: when a pooled connection meets an unresponsive peer (a stuck process, a network broken midway) and the caller's ctx has no deadline, the query waits until the caller gives up. Measured, setting this to 1s still waited: 30s later it had not returned — the statement never reached the server, which therefore had nothing to time. The only thing governing that stretch is the caller's deadline: pass a ctx with one through CWithCtx, and measured with 200ms it returned in 200ms. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

PrepareStmt.description: caches executed SQL as prepared statements and reuses them for the same SQL later. false by default. Measured on local loopback over 2000 runs of the same parameterized query: MySQL 8.0 went from about 180µs to 94µs each (without it the driver does prepare / execute / close, three round trips per statement) and PostgreSQL 16 from about 100µs to 85µs (pgx caches statements anyway, so the difference is small). The cache size and expiry use GORM's defaults (unlimited, 1h). Behind a connection pooler such as PgBouncer (transaction mode especially), measure in that environment before turning it on.

SkipDefaultTransaction.description: stops wrapping a single Create / Update / Delete in a transaction. false by default (GORM's default: it wraps). What it saves is the BEGIN / COMMIT round trips: measured on local loopback over 500 single Creates, PostgreSQL 16 went from about 500µs to 230µs each and MySQL 8.0 from about 1.0ms to 0.9ms. The cost is that writes inside hooks such as BeforeCreate no longer share the main statement's fate; an explicit Transaction is unaffected.

SlowThreshold.description: logs a warn line for any statement slower than this. Defaults to 3s, needs Log on, and 0 records none. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

TLS.description: decides whether the database connection uses TLS. Off by default (TLS parameters written in the DSN still apply). The fields and rules are shared by the modules, see xtls.Config. With it on, TLS is decided entirely by this block: certificates are always verified and there is **no fallback to plaintext**. Writing TLS parameters in the DSN as well (PostgreSQL's sslmode, sslrootcert and the other ssl-prefixed ones, MySQL's tls) is a configuration error — two places saying different things means whichever wins makes the other pointless. How the drivers take it, and the measured behavior, are in xtls/README.md.

CAFile.description: is the CA certificate used to verify the server certificate (PEM, several are allowed). It defaults to empty, which uses the system roots. When it is set, **only** the CAs in that file are accepted and the system roots no longer take part. A self-signed certificate goes here.

CertFile.description: is the client certificate (PEM), set together with KeyFile when the server wants mutual authentication. It defaults to empty.

Enable.description: turns TLS on. It defaults to false. The fields below only take effect while it is on, and setting them without it fails startup -- that is most likely a forgotten Enable, and connecting in plaintext would be worse than an error.

KeyFile.description: is the client private key (PEM), set together with CertFile. It defaults to empty.

ServerName.description: is the name the server certificate is verified against. It defaults to empty, which takes the host part of the connection address; set it when connecting by IP to a certificate that names a domain.

Trace.description: decides whether the OpenTelemetry plugin is attached. On by default. Without tracing installed it produces noop spans at negligible cost, which is why it is on by default. The attributes follow OTel's database semantic conventions v1.43.0 (db.system.name, db.namespace, db.query.text, db.operation.name, server.address / server.port). db.query.text carries placeholders and no parameter values; a server-side error records the error code alone (db.response.status_code).

XHttp.description: is the outbound HTTP client configuration. Unlike xgorm / xredis there are no several instances here: an HTTP client connects to no external resource, works unconfigured, and one shared connection pool and timeout is enough. A scenario needing a second set of parameters builds one with New directly.

DialKeepAlive.description: is the TCP keep-alive probe interval. It defaults to 30s. It is the one duration where a negative value is meaningful: the standard library's net.Dialer takes a negative value as "send no probes", which is why it is not in Validate's non-negative check. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

DialTimeout.description: is the timeout for establishing a TCP connection. It defaults to 30s. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

IdleConnTimeout.description: is how long an idle connection is kept. It defaults to 90s, as in the standard library. When the downstream (or a load balancer in between) closes an idle connection first, a request reusing it at exactly that moment fails: measured with a 200ms server-side idle timeout and request intervals around 200ms, 27 of 300 POSTs failed (connection reset by peer / use of closed network connection); GETs are resent automatically on a new connection and none of 200 failed. So it has to be shorter than the downstream's keep-alive timeout. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

Log.description: says whether one log line is recorded per logical request (once, after every retry has finished). It defaults to off. It records the method, host, path, status code, duration and attempt count, plus the error on failure; the query string, the fragment, the userinfo, the headers and the body are never recorded, and the query string is removed from the URLs in the error text too. An error from resty (a transport error, a failing SetResult, a refused redirect) and a 5xx are recorded at warn. With it on, resty's own lines on the retry path (one WARN per attempt, one ERROR once used up) are no longer printed and a request is just this one line; a SetLogger of your own is unaffected. A request dump from SetDebug(true) is not covered, and its query string and headers reach the log as they are. The fields and the measurements are in xhttp/README.md.

MaxConnsPerHost.description: is the upper bound on connections per host (those in use included). It defaults to 0, unlimited, as in the standard library. Unlimited means as many as the concurrency asks for: measured against a downstream answering after 300ms with 200 concurrent requests, it received 200 new connections; another 200 right after reused only the 10 of MaxIdleConnsPerHost and opened 190 more. As the downstream slows, the connection count rises with the concurrency and may exhaust the peer's connections or this machine's ports. Set positive, excess requests queue for a connection, and that wait counts against Timeout and the caller's ctx.

MaxIdleConns.description: is the global maximum number of idle connections. It defaults to 100.

MaxIdleConnsPerHost.description: is the maximum number of idle connections per host. It defaults to 10. The standard library's default is 2, which is too small for a service calling only a few downstreams: connections would be rebuilt over and over and the tail latency would be all handshakes.

Metric.description: says whether the outbound request metrics are exported (by method, target and status code). It defaults to on.

RetryCount.description: is the number of retries. It defaults to 0, meaning no retry.

RetryMaxWaitTime.description: is the upper bound on the retry wait. It defaults to 2s. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

RetryOnlyIdempotent.description: says whether only idempotent methods are retried. It defaults to on. A transport-layer timeout cannot tell "the request never reached the server" from "the server finished and the response was lost", so resending a POST may mean a duplicate order or a duplicate charge. Turn it off once the endpoint is confirmed idempotent (carrying an idempotency key, say). A condition added with AddRetryCondition cannot put a POST with no response back either (xhttp vetoes that in RetryAfter); what it can put back is one retrying on a status code after a response arrived (a 5xx, say) -- vetoing there could only replace the response with an invented error, so such a condition has to check the method itself. A SetRetryAfter of your own replaces this gate. Either way, a request whose body is an io.Reader is never retried: the first attempt read it to the end and a resend would have an empty body.

RetryWaitTime.description: is the initial retry wait. It defaults to 100ms. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

SlowThreshold.description: records one warn line when the whole logical request (retries and backoff included) takes longer than this. It defaults to 1s, requires Log, and 0 records nothing. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

TLS.description: is the TLS setup for outbound https requests: a self-signed CA, a client certificate for mutual authentication, the name to verify against. It defaults to unconfigured, using the standard library's defaults (the system roots, no client certificate). The fields and rules are shared across modules, see xtls.Config. It governs https:// requests only and never upgrades http:// to TLS. It applies to **every** https request this client sends: with CAFile configured only that CA is accepted, so an https downstream on the public internet no longer verifies; and ServerName verifies every downstream against that one name. So this is for the client that calls one kind of internal downstream only; to call the public internet as well, build another one with New.

CAFile.description: is the CA certificate used to verify the server certificate (PEM, several are allowed). It defaults to empty, which uses the system roots. When it is set, **only** the CAs in that file are accepted and the system roots no longer take part. A self-signed certificate goes here.

CertFile.description: is the client certificate (PEM), set together with KeyFile when the server wants mutual authentication. It defaults to empty.

Enable.description: turns TLS on. It defaults to false. The fields below only take effect while it is on, and setting them without it fails startup -- that is most likely a forgotten Enable, and connecting in plaintext would be worse than an error.

KeyFile.description: is the client private key (PEM), set together with CertFile. It defaults to empty.

ServerName.description: is the name the server certificate is verified against. It defaults to empty, which takes the host part of the connection address; set it when connecting by IP to a certificate that names a domain.

Timeout.description: is the timeout of one attempt. It defaults to 60s. 0 means "never time out", not "use some default": with an unresponsive peer the request hangs forever. Note that it governs one attempt, not one logical request: with RetryCount on, the worst case is (RetryCount+1) x Timeout plus the backoff waits (measured at a full 1.24s with Timeout=300ms and RetryCount=3). To cap the whole logical request, use the caller's ctx -- both the retry backoff and each attempt honor it (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)

Trace.description: says whether a Span is opened for an outbound request. It defaults to on. It governs the Span only. With it off, traceparent, baggage and the forwarded headers from XTrace.ForwardHeaders still travel downstream (the trace identifiers come from the upstream, or from a Span opened elsewhere in this process): not recording a Span for this hop must not break the whole trace and the forwarding here.

XKafka.description: is this module's configuration. There are two forms

Brokers.description: are the seed broker addresses, host:port. It is required and has no default. They are only seeds: once connected to any one of them, franz-go learns the whole cluster's brokers from the metadata.

ClientID.description: is the client.id sent to the brokers, which the broker-side logs, quotas and monitoring use to tell clients apart. It defaults to empty: one built through the framework falls back to XApp.Name, and with neither configured it stays empty, which franz-go sends as its own default kgo (measured on v1.21.7). No name is invented for it -- startup writes one WARN instead, since every service on the cluster going by kgo cannot be told apart in the brokers' request logs or quotas. A direct call to New reads no XApp at all.

Consumer.description: holds the settings of the consuming side, applying to every Consume on this cluster.

ResetOffset.description: is where to start when a consumer group consumes a partition for the first time (with no committed offset), or when the committed offset has already been cleaned up: latest (only what arrives afterwards) or earliest (from the oldest message still retained). It defaults to latest. franz-go's default is earliest (measured on v1.21.7): a newly deployed consumer group would process every historical message still retained in the topic. This module defaults to latest, at the cost of a new group, or a group starting just after the topic was created, never processing what was written before -- configure earliest when those are wanted.

SessionTimeout.description: is how long the broker waits for a heartbeat before it takes this consumer for gone and hands its partitions to another member of the group. Zero keeps franz-go's default, which is 45s (measured on v1.21.7: cfg.sessionTimeout in pkg/kgo/config.go). It is the time a partition stops being consumed after a process is killed outright, and nothing shortens it: a process that exits through its stop hooks leaves the group on its way out and its partitions move at once, while one that was SIGKILLed, fenced or had its host disappear is only noticed when this runs out. items.description: is a per-domain header forwarding rule. The matching headers are forwarded only when the target domain matches one of the patterns in Domains.

Domains.description: are the domain patterns, supporting exact matches and a wildcard prefix (*.example.com).

Headers.description: are the headers to forward under this rule.

ForwardHeaders.description: are the headers forwarded to every domain. There are none by default. Only values from a trusted peer are accepted: with xgin that is whatever is in XGin.TrustedProxies (XEcho.TrustedProxies for xecho), which by default trusts only the private ranges (load balancers, a K8s Ingress and Pods) and not a direct connection from the internet. The reasoning is in HeaderPropagator.Extract.

SampleRatio.description: is the sampling ratio for root Spans, in [0, 1]. It defaults to 1. Out of range or NaN fails startup. It only governs traces with no upstream: when an upstream sends a sampling decision (traceparent's sampled bit) that decision is followed, even at a ratio of 1 -- otherwise a trace an upstream deliberately dropped would be picked back up here. Writing 0 means "sample no new trace at all", while Spans are still created and TraceIDs are still generated and forwarded -- which is how to give downstream services a TraceID without storing Spans locally. To produce no Spans at all (a noop provider), use Enable: false, which is a different thing.

ShutdownTimeout.description: is the upper bound on waiting for Spans to be exported during shutdown. It defaults to 5s and must be greater than 0. There has to be an upper bound: with the export endpoint unreachable, Shutdown blocks forever, and without a deadline that is a hang on exit. Likewise, 0 does not mean "no limit" but "do not wait at all": Shutdown receives an already expired context, and the Spans still in the buffer are dropped outright. (a duration, written as 30s / 1500ms / 1h30m; a bare number fails startup)
